note: Hand-written per-set editorial. One entry per set in the tracker. This file exists because templated set pages (63% identical sentences, measured 2026-08-07) are exactly what AdSense calls low-value content -- every set page must say something that is only true of that set. Grounded in stable facts only: set identity, chase-card identities from our own tracker, release windows, structural observations. No live prices here; those belong to the data layer. Written by hand -- do not machine-generate entries, and never copy a sentence between sets (guard S3 enforces both).

OP-01.heading: The set everything else gets measured against
OP-01.desc: OP-01 Romance Dawn guide: why the game's first Japanese booster box behaves like a vintage product, and the parallel Luffy that leads it.
body: Romance Dawn is the One Piece Card Game's first main set, and its sealed boxes behave less like a current product and more like an early-era collectible: the original December 2022 print run has long since left retail, so secondary-market supply only shrinks. The chase side is led by the parallel-art Monkey D. Luffy 003 — the closest thing this game has to a flagship rookie card — with the parallel Zoro and Law from the same cycle right behind it.

Because it opens the numbering, OP-01 is also where collectors start when they work backwards through the run, which keeps steady demand on a box that stopped being printed years ago. We track it daily like every other set, but read its swings with that vintage lens: moves here are about scarcity, not pull-rate news.

OP-02.heading: Marineford, and the manga rare that defined a card class
OP-02.desc: OP-02 Paramount War: the Ace manga-art parallel that made the manga rare a chase class of its own, with Garp and Sanji alternates behind it.
body: Paramount War puts the Marineford war on cardboard, and one card from it changed how the whole game is collected: the manga-art parallel of Portgas D. Ace. That card made the comic-panel treatment a chase class in its own right — every later set's manga rare gets compared to it. Alternate-art Sanji and Garp fill out the top of the box.

As the second main set its supply story is nearly as tight as OP-01's. When Ace moves, the sealed box tends to follow; few boxes in the run are as single-card-driven as this one, and the graded population of that Ace is the number that decides whether the premium holds.

OP-03.heading: Enies Lobby's odd couple: a masked sniper and a wanted poster
OP-03.desc: OP-03 Pillars of Strength guide: Sogeking's manga alternate and the Luffy wanted-poster frame that started a design tradition.
body: Pillars of Strength covers the Water 7 and Enies Lobby stretch, and its two signature cards could not be more different: the manga-art Sogeking — Usopp in his sniper alter ego — and a Luffy framed as his own wanted poster, an art treatment the game kept returning to in later sets. The alternate-art Nami here is a staple of female-character collections.

The set was printed in the game's first summer, while demand was still being discovered, so boxes from this window carry the same shrinking-supply logic as the two sets before it. In our chase table the value is spread wider than in Ace's set — a board of mid-strength cards rather than one giant.

OP-04.heading: The schemers' set
OP-04.desc: OP-04 Kingdoms of Intrigue: manga-art Sabo out front, SP-treatment Hancock and Law behind, closing out the quiet half of 2023.
body: Kingdoms of Intrigue is the villains-and-plotters chapter of the run, and its top end reflects it: manga-art Sabo up front, with special-treatment SP versions of Boa Hancock and Trafalgar Law behind him. SP cards — stamped character favorites folded into later boxes — are how this game keeps older fan favorites circulating, and two of them anchor this set's premium tier.

It closed the third quarter of 2023, one set before the release that changed the game's economics entirely, so OP-04 tends to be read as the last quiet box of the early era. That framing matters when you compare its chart to what came next.

OP-05.heading: The watershed box
OP-05.desc: OP-05 Awakening of the New Era: the Gear 5 set and its gold-stamped signature Luffy — the card that pulled the game into the mainstream.
body: If a single set moved One Piece cards from hobby corner to mainstream collecting, it is this one. Awakening of the New Era lands on the Gear 5 arc, and its chase — the alternate-art Luffy 119 with the gold-stamped signature — became the most talked-about card in the game's history. Law and Luffy alternates deepen the list, but this box's economics hang on one card to a degree no earlier set matched.

That concentration cuts both ways: when the flagship Luffy is strong, sealed OP-05 looks unstoppable, and when its graded supply builds, the box cools with it. The per-card rows under the chase table are the thing to watch here, more than the box price alone.

OP-06.heading: Zoro's turn, Robin's throwback
OP-06.desc: OP-06 Wings of the Captain: manga-art Zoro leads, Robin appears as Ms. All Sunday, and a treasure-rare Nami completes the podium.
body: Wings of the Captain hands the flagship spot to the manga-art Roronoa Zoro and backs it with one of the run's best character ideas: Nico Robin printed under her old Baroque Works identity, Ms. All Sunday, in SP treatment. A treasure-rare Nami completes the podium.

Three different card classes at the top — manga, SP, treasure rare — spread this box's value across more than one card, the opposite of its predecessor's one-card economy. That balance is why OP-06 keeps coming up as a first Japanese box for collectors crossing over from the English game.

OP-07.heading: Egghead arrives, and Hancock rules it
OP-07.desc: OP-07 500 Years in the Future: the parallel manga Boa Hancock 051 leads the Egghead set, ahead of O-Nami and a treasure-rare Law.
body: 500 Years in the Future is the Egghead-arc set, but its market identity belongs to Boa Hancock: her parallel manga-art 051 is the strongest female-character chase in the main-set run to that point, leading the table ahead of the O-Nami SP and a treasure-rare Law.

Sets whose top card is not a protagonist behave differently — demand comes from character collectors as much as players, and that base is loyal. Hancock's population growth at the graders is the number to watch if you hold this box sealed; the grading figures further down the page come straight from our ledger.

OP-08.heading: The old guard takes the top slot
OP-08.desc: OP-08 Two Legends: parallel manga Rayleigh out-chases every protagonist, with an Ace SP and treasure-rare Luffy close behind.
body: Two Legends is exactly what its name promises — a set built around the game's elder statesmen. The parallel manga-art Silvers Rayleigh leads it, one of the few times a mentor-generation character out-chases every protagonist in the box, with an Ace SP and a treasure-rare Luffy close behind.

Rayleigh chases age well because his premium card count across the whole run is small; there are only so many to collect. That, more than arc hype, is what gives this autumn-2024 box its particular floor — and it makes the reprint section below worth reading more carefully than usual.

OP-09.heading: One card: Roger
OP-09.desc: OP-09 Emperors in the New World is the Gol D. Roger set — the Pirate King's chase, with manga Luffy and Shanks in the second tier.
body: Emperors in the New World gathers the yonko era into one box, and the market read it instantly: the Gol D. Roger chase is the card, with the manga-art Luffy 119 and a manga Shanks forming the second tier. A Pirate King card topping a set about emperors is as clean as set design gets.

In our table this set's value curve is steep — a big step from first place down to the rest. Steep-curve boxes reward buyers who care about the one hit and punish those who valued the median pull, which is worth knowing before comparing it against flatter sets like OP-03.

OP-10.heading: Law's set, Whitebeard's shadow
OP-10.desc: OP-10 Royal Blood: a manga-art Law 119 tops the lineage-themed set, with an Edward Newgate SP and treasure-rare Ace in support.
body: Royal Blood is the lineage set — family names and inherited wills — and its chase list leans on two permanent fan favorites: a manga-art Trafalgar Law 119 at the top and an Edward Newgate SP behind it, with a treasure-rare Ace keeping the Marineford thread alive.

Between this appearance and his earlier SP and treasure-rare printings, Law holds buyers across sets in a way few characters other than Luffy manage. Boxes from spring 2025 are recent enough that some retail supply still exists, so the sealed premium here runs thinner than on anything from 2023.

OP-11.heading: All in on one character
OP-11.desc: OP-11 A Fist of Divine Speed: gold SP, standard SP and manga Luffy stack the top three — a one-character box, priced like one.
body: A Fist of Divine Speed does something no earlier main set did so nakedly: its top three chases are all the same character. Gold-stamped SP Luffy, standard SP Luffy, manga-art Luffy — the entire premium end of the box is one man.

That makes OP-11 the purest single-character bet in the run. If Gear-5-era Luffy demand stays where it is, the box needs nothing else; if it fades, there is no second act in the chase list to catch it. We flag concentration like this because a box's risk profile lives in the shape of its table, not in its title.

OP-12.heading: Blackbeard, twice
OP-12.desc: OP-12 Legacy of the Master: gold and silver SP Blackbeards share the summit, with manga-art Jewelry Bonney as the wildcard third.
body: Legacy of the Master hands its top end to the game's great villain: Marshall D. Teach appears twice at the summit, in gold-stamped and silver-stamped SP treatments — a two-tier pairing that stands out even in a run full of variant experiments. The manga-art Jewelry Bonney behind them is the kind of left-field third chase that quietly builds a following.

Villain-led boxes are rarer than protagonist-led ones and their buyers skew collector over player. Watch how the two Teach variants price against each other in the table — that gold-versus-silver gap is a small market signal no other set currently offers.

OP-13.heading: The Gorosei era opens
OP-13.desc: OP-13 Carrying on His Will: a Five Elders parallel tops the set, ahead of Ace's wanted poster and the red manga Luffy variant.
body: Carrying on His Will is where the endgame cast arrives: the parallel-art St. Marcus Mars — one of the Five Elders — tops the chase table, a striking result for a brand-new antagonist. Behind him sit an Ace wanted-poster frame and the red manga-art Luffy, the scarcer red-stamped cousin of the standard manga class, which we track as its own variant.

Brand-new-character chases carry discovery risk in both directions: no price history, no population base, everything still being decided. That is what makes this late-2025 box one of the more interesting ones in our daily data — and why sold prices deserve even more weight over asking prices here than usual.

OP-14.heading: Buggy on top, and the run starts quoting itself
OP-14.desc: OP-14 The Azure Sea's Seven: gold SP Buggy leads the chase list, and stamped reprints of older hits fill much of the top ten.
body: The Azure Sea's Seven produced the fandom's favorite market fact: Buggy — the clown — leads the chase table, in gold-stamped and standard SP forms. Behind the joke is a structural shift worth noticing: much of this set's top ten consists of stamped reprints of older hits, cards carrying OP-09 and PRB-02 numbers. The run has started quoting its own back catalogue.

Stamped reprints behave differently from originals — they add supply to a character while remaining distinct collectibles, and their prices key off the original printing. A box this recent is still settling, so treat the live table above as the current read rather than a settled ranking.

OP-15.heading: Skypiea's god gets his card
OP-15.desc: OP-15 Adventure on Kami's Island: manga-art Enel finally leads a set, with a stamped Koby crossover and a Hancock SP behind him.
body: Adventure on Kami's Island takes the run to Skypiea, and Enel — the villain the fandom never stopped quoting — finally gets a manga-art chase worthy of the memes. A Koby carrying its EB-04 stamp and another Hancock SP complete the top three.

This is one of the newest main sets in the tracker, which means the data window behind this page is short: fewer completed sales, thinner population counts, wider error bars. We publish what we have and blank what we cannot verify — read every figure on a set this young as a first reading, not a verdict.

OP-16.heading: Three admirals, one cycle
OP-16.desc: OP-16 The Time of Battle: manga-art Sakazuki, Kuzan and Borsalino form a complete admiral cycle at the top of the newest main set.
body: The Time of Battle is the newest main set in the tracker, and its top three form something the run had not produced before in our table: a complete themed cycle. Manga-art Sakazuki, Kuzan and Borsalino — the three original admirals — sit together at the summit, and cycle chases invite completionism: plenty of buyers here want all three or none.

A box this fresh moves on opening-volume news more than anything durable. Our sell-through and auction figures for OP-16 will mean far more by autumn than they do today; the honest read is "watch", and this page refreshes daily while the picture forms.

EB-01.heading: The extra-booster formula, first try
EB-01.desc: EB-01 Memorial Collection: what an extra booster is, and how manga-art Chopper became the face of this reprint-heavy box.
body: Memorial Collection introduced the extra-booster format to the Japanese run: a smaller checklist, heavy on reprints and celebration cards, sold as a look back at the game's opening stretch. Its market surprise was Tony Tony Chopper — the manga-art alternate became the face of the box — with a Mr. 2 Bon Kurei alternate as the run's best fan-service pick.

Extra boosters live or die on their alternates, because the base cards are known quantities. EB-01's alternates aged well, which is why this nominally minor product keeps a permanent place in our daily tracking alongside the main sets.

EB-02.heading: The anniversary box
EB-02.desc: EB-02 Anime 25th Collection: the anime's quarter-century celebration set, led by a Hancock SP and a nostalgic manga-art Luffy.
body: Anime 25th Collection is the celebration box, built for the anime's quarter-century with art direction that leans nostalgic. A Boa Hancock SP leads it, the manga-art Luffy 061 sits close behind, and a Chopper SP holds the mascot slot.

Anniversary products pull in buyers who otherwise never touch the card game, and that widened base shows in how often this box surfaces in our deals module. The long-term question is the usual one for celebration sets — whether demand outlives the birthday — and the daily numbers on this page are how we are finding out.

EB-03.heading: The all-heroines experiment
EB-03.desc: EB-03 Heroine's Edition: an all-female premium end — Robin, Nami and Hancock SPs — and the distinct buyer base that comes with it.
body: Heroine's Edition is the run's clearest demographic experiment: a box whose entire premium end is female characters — Nico Robin, Nami and Boa Hancock in SP treatment. No other product in the game concentrates that collector segment so completely.

Products aimed at character collectors rather than players sell through differently: steadier, less tied to tournament news, more sensitive to gift-season timing. It released in February 2026, so our ledger on it is still young — the auction data lower on this page is the least filtered view of how the experiment is landing.

PRB-01.heading: The best-of box
PRB-01.desc: PRB-01 Premium Booster explained: curated stamped reprints of the run's biggest hits, and why its supply rhythm is unusual.
body: Premium Booster is a different kind of product from a numbered set: a curated reprint box whose chase list is older hits wearing new stamps. Our table for it is led by a Luffy carrying its original OP-05 119 number, a Chopper with an EB-01 stamp, and a Nami from OP-01 — the run's greatest-hits album.

In Japan, premium boosters have moved through narrower channels than open retail, which gives PRB products a supply rhythm unlike the main sets: tight at release, loosening in waves. Read its price history against that cadence, not against a numbered set's.

PRB-02.heading: Greatest hits, volume two
PRB-02.desc: PRB-02 Premium Booster: the second reprint-selection box — a stamped Sanji manga art and the Gum-Gum Giant alternate lead it.
body: The second Premium Booster repeats the formula with a different tracklist: its top end carries a Sanji manga-art with its original OP-06 119 number, the Gum-Gum Giant alternate art, and a stamped SP Luffy from EB-02. Selection boxes like this are effectively Bandai's editorial statement about which cards mattered.

Because every chase here is a restamped known quantity, PRB-02 prices lean on their originals: the stamped copy usually trades under the original print, and the gap between the two is a useful scarcity signal. Both versions sit in our per-card tracker — compare them before paying either price.
